rss_0_1789506146.title: ‘I believed the hype’: the white South Africans denied refugee status in the US
rss_0_1789506146.text:
When Donald Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would accept Afrikaners from South Africa as refugees, many white South Africans who believed that they were victims of racism in their country thought that their prayers had been answered.

However, in the past few months, dozens of applicants to the refugee programme have been rejected, with many left dismayed and confused as to why they would be left to face what Trump has falsely claimed is a “white genocide” in South Africa.

After Trump’s February 2025 executive order announcing the resettlement programme, which was expanded to include members of a “racial minority”, the first group of 68 white South Africans arrived in the US that May. The US also shut down the refugee programme for anyone else fleeing war and persecution.

Since then, more than 13,000 have moved to the US, according to state department figures. Arrivals are also accelerating, with more than 2,600 admitted in August.

Afrikaners, descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime repressed the black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.

Since the end of apartheid more than 30 years ago, affirmative action policies have helped to create a black elite and middle class. But about 38% of black South Africans are unemployed, compared with 9% of white South Africans, according to official data.

View image in fullscreen The first group of Afrikaners arrived in the US under Trump’s refugee programme in early May 2025. Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Meanwhile, the “black economic empowerment” policies, along with high crime rates that affect everyone, have fostered a feeling among some white South Africans that they are now the victims of racial discrimination.

The racist far right has also long highlighted brutal murders of white South African farmers, claiming them as evidence of white people being targeted. Official crime data does not show farmers or white people experiencing crime at higher rates. That has not stopped Trump amplifying these claims, in the face of the South African government’s furious rebuttals.

On 30 June, Facebook and WhatsApp groups for prospective and successful refugee applicants began to light up with news that people had begun to receive rejection letters.

“We are writing to inform you that, following review, USCIS [US Citizenship and Immigration Services] found your application to be ineligible for continued processing for resettlement to the United States at this time. This cannot be appealed,” the letters said, according to multiple rejections seen by the Guardian.

It is unclear how many have been found ineligible. USCIS did not provide data on the total number of refugee applications and rejections. One WhatsApp group set up to support rejects, called Hope beyond the Letter, had 311 members as of 10 September, according to one of the administrators, who noted that the membership fluctuated.

While the ineligibility letters did not give reasons for rejection, some applicants were given more information after making Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests. The WhatsApp group administrator, a 64-year-old freelance TV professional, who did not want his identity disclosed, found that his case was initially “recommended for approval”. However, the recommendation was reversed because his ex-girlfriend, whom he had applied with, had a marijuana conviction.

“I cried like a baby,” he said, of receiving the rejection letter on 30 June, having finished the screening process in November. “It was something I actually believed was attainable. I believed the hype.”

View image in fullscreen During a meeting in May 2025, Donald Trump ambushed Cyril Ramaphosa with printed-out news articles supposedly pointing to a ‘white genocide’ in South Africa. In this image the US president is in fact holding up a photograph of Ebola victims being buried in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Photograph: Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA

Pieter and Liesl (not their real names) were told they were “conditionally approved” as refugees last November. Both are Afrikaners who had a grandparent killed on a farm and were managing a farm when they applied to become refugees.

Pieter said he was convicted of trespassing in 2014, for which he said he paid a fine and did not go to court. He was granted multiple temporary visas to work on farms in the US between 2011 and 2024.

The couple’s youngest daughter was born in the US and is a US citizen. In the response to their FoI request, they noticed that USCIS had recorded her nationality as South African and incorrectly said that she would be left behind if they moved to the US as refugees.

They had already sold their house, car and many of their possessions when they received a rejection letter on 24 July. “We have to start all over again,” Pieter said.

Another applicant blamed not being able to speak in his native Afrikaans for what he claimed were misunderstandings that led to him and his wife being rejected. The reasons given in response to their FoI request were “crime involving moral turpitude” and “commission of acts of torture or extra judicial killing”.

The 67-year-old had admitted to shooting at least one black person when working as a security guard in 1995, but said it was in self-defence while responding to the mass break-in of an alcohol shop. “I was thoroughly investigated by the authorities,” he said. “I was not charged, because I did not break the law.”

In an emailed response that did not address specific cases, the USCIS spokesperson Zach Kahler said: “The Department of Homeland Security is committed to resettling Afrikaner refugees who are being persecuted by the South African government.

“[USCIS] reviews each refugee application on a case-by-case basis … [and] notifies aliens found ineligible for continued processing through the US Refugee Admissions Program, including those found ineligible for public safety concerns or criminal histories. This cannot be appealed. This administration will always prioritize the safety and welfare of the American people.”

rss_1_1789506146.title: Ebola outbreak in DRC has peaked, say authorities, as infection rates slow
rss_1_1789506146.text:
Authorities in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have announced that the Ebola outbreak ravaging parts of the country has reached its peak.

For the first time since the epidemic was declared in May, the numbers of people becoming infected is slowing down, according to officials.

Stressing that strict adherence to preventive measures needed to be kept in place, Samuel Roger Kamba, the Congolese health minister, said there was a decline in transmission of the Bundibugyo variant of Ebola.

“We are fighting a very dangerous virus that is killing many of our people. Today, we can say that the outbreak is under control,” he said. “At one point, we were recording about 120 cases per day; today, we’re seeing about 80 per day. So the number of new cases is decreasing every day.

“It has been more than 22 days since 10 of the 62 health zones have reported new cases. And so we can now definitively remove six health zones from the list because they have gone more than 42 days without new cases, and we can remove four health zones that have gone more than 21 days without a new case,” Kamba said.

Last week, the Sud-Ubangi region, on the DRC’s borders with Congo-Brazzaville and Central African Republic, became the sixth province to report the disease.

The Bundibugyo virus outbreak was declared by Congolese authorities on 15 May and is concentrated primarily in Ituri province, where ongoing conflict has created challenging conditions for those responding to the disease. It is the 17th outbreak of Ebola in the DRC since the highly contagious disease was first identified and named in 1976.

No effective treatment for the Bundibugyo variant has been found so far but there are clinical trials in the region. The DRC received more than 70,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine last month, which is the only approved treatment for the more common Zaire Ebola virus.

View image in fullscreen Children read an information poster about Ebola in Bunia, Ituri province, which is one of the areas of the DRC hardest hit by the outbreak. Photograph: Gradel Muyisa Mumbere/Reuters

According to the latest data from the Congolese health ministry, the number of confirmed cases stood at more than 7,200, including more than 3,475 deaths, as of 14 September.

While welcoming the progress made, Iracan Gratien de Saint-Nicolas, an MP for Bunia, warned against what he called “triumphalism” and stressed that efforts must intensify to show people that the disease was under control.

Gratien Iracan called for lessons to be learned from failures in epidemiological surveillance that contributed to the rapid spread of the disease.

The MP also expressed some scepticism over the government announcement. “Claims that an epidemic is under control must be supported by objective indicators. If the indicators show that the epidemic is indeed under control, let’s make them public. Transparency in the data will strengthen public confidence,” he said.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every fortnight Sign up to Global Dispatch Get a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development team Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

He warned that some indicators that showed an epidemic was under control seemed to have been omitted by the DRC authorities, such as a sustained decline in new cases (over seven to 21 days), a decrease in deaths, a reduction in areas with active transmission, the majority of new cases originating from contacts already identified, and a high rate of contact tracing, as well as dignified and safe burials.

Early last month, Jean Kaseya, the director general of the African Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, visited Bunia – capital of Ituri and a centre of the current Ebola outbreak – and said then that there was no way of knowing when the peak might be reached but that containment and contact tracing were still not effective enough.

Kaseya said: “A large portion of the mortality – 60 to 70% of deaths – comes from the community. The list of contacts we have just keeps growing. Epidemiologists say we’ve reached the peak when all cases come from the list of contacts.”

In Rwampara, a town in Ituri, people are exhausted from the past few months of living with the dread of the disease. Léa Munyere, 36, a mother of four, said she was relieved that the health authorities had announced that Ebola was under control. Two of her close friends had died and she was still struggling to come to terms with the loss, she said.

“We hope the disease will soon be declared over. It has robbed us of the people we cherish so much since it was first reported,” she said. “We just want to get back to our normal lives.”

rss_2_1789506146.title: The London hospital funded by donors who invested in the slave trade
rss_2_1789506146.text:
Inside the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, alongside stately portraits of the apostle from whom London’s oldest hospital takes its name and King Henry VIII, extravagant commemorative boards adorn the walls.

The Great Hall was a grand, formal space where governors weighed their philanthropic donations and drafted their wills, many while investing in the stock of companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Today, many of those donors are commemorated in acrylic gold paint on the boards.

The Register of British Slave Traders, a joint venture between Lancaster University, the University of Manchester and University College London, includes biographical data on every known investor in Britain’s transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people from the 16th to 19th centuries.

It reveals how wealthy individuals, often enriched by the proceeds from racialised chattel enslavement, donated to hundreds of church parishes and helped to fund schools, hospitals and charities across the country.

Prof William Pettigrew, who led the project, said the register had established connections with roughly 900 organisations. “Most of those organisations sought to improve the lives of ordinary Britons,” he added.

The register reveals at least 50 people with deep financial ties to Barts who are directly linked to this history.

Among the names etched on to the boards in the Great Hall is Sir Jeffrey Jeffreys, a London merchant who left an unspecified sum to the hospital in his will. In 1694, the Jeffreys-funded ship Hannibal, commanded by Capt Thomas Phillips, docked in Barbados. This concluded a harrowing journey in which only 372 of the 700 enslaved African people bought at Whydah (Ouidah in modern-day Benin) survived the Atlantic crossing.

View image in fullscreen The grand Hogarth Stair, which leads to the Great Hall, adorned with paintings depicting healing. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen Ornate boards adorn the walls of the Great Hall in Barts, where governors recorded their philanthropic donations, many while investing in the companies built on the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen The church of St Bartholomew the Less, in the grounds of Barts hospital. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen A portrait of King Henry VIII in the Great Hall of St Bartholomew’s North Wing, surrounded by the boards commemorating the hospital’s benefactors. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

Phillips’s journal, one of the few surviving records of the voyage, details the horrors onboard, where captives were subjected to branding and calculated psychological cruelty. “Then we marked the slaves we had bought in the breast or shoulder, with a hot iron, having the letter of the ship’s name on it,” he wrote. The Africans on his ship, he recorded, held “a more dreadful apprehension of Barbadoes than we have of hell”.

Phillips recalled using African overseers, who were enslaved themselves, to keep order, whipping any plotters of mutiny. There were grave consequences of the squalid conditions on the ship; many who died on the Hannibal were killed by smallpox, dysentery, starvation and suicide. Some were thrown overboard when dead or dying to prevent the spread of disease and to protect profits.

The voyage’s mortality rate was close to 50%, cementing its place as one of the deadliest crossings in the history of the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.

View image in fullscreen A diagram of a ship showing the cramped conditions in which enslaved Africans were trafficked. Composite: Guardian

The 1694 Hannibal crossing was one of 13 to which Jeffreys was financially linked. The London merchant was a director of the Royal African Company from 1684-86, and from 1692-98. His latter term coincided with the end of the company’s royal monopoly on trading enslaved Africans, from which he profited handsomely. He also inherited a fortune from his tobacco-trading uncle, John Jeffreys, in 1688. During Jeffrey Jeffreys’ time with the RAC, the organisation made 170 crossings.

Others commemorated at Barts have links to the trafficking of enslaved Africans. Edward Colston, whose statue was toppled by Black Lives Matter protesters in Bristol in June 2020, appears in the register. William Prichard, once president of Barts and a leading City merchant, bought £600 of RAC stock in January 1678.

Sir Robert Geffrye, who left money to the hospital and other philanthropic causes in his will, was a substantial investor in the trafficking of enslaved Africans, selling £1,600 (the equivalent of £350,000 today) of RAC stock on 5 January 1692 alone. Diane Abbott, the MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, has called for the removal of Geffrye’s statue at the Museum of the Home in Hoxton.

These connections run through the heart of the City of London’s political structure, with several lord mayors commemorated in the Great Hall. Sir William Humphreys, who left legacies to three London hospitals including Barts, sat on the RAC’s court of assistants from 1683-85 and from 1688-90. In 1711, he attended Board of Trade hearings on the company’s operations on the west African coast, three years before he became lord mayor.

His predecessor, Samuel Stanier, who also left money to Barts in his will, sold off most of his substantial £4,000 holding in the RAC in February 1698, before his lord mayoralty started in 1713.

After the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans became more formalised and was a lucrative source of funds for merchants.

View image in fullscreen Several leading City merchants who invested in companies linked to the enslavement of African people are commemorated in the Great Hall at Barts. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen After the British crown was restored in 1660, the trafficking of enslaved Africans formalised to become a lucrative source of funds for merchants. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen The Great Hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message. Its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – are tied to themes of healthcare. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen The stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored last year and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda. Photograph: Wayne Crichlow/The Guardian

The private banker Sir Robert Vyner (also known as Viner) became a central figure in the City and was lord mayor of London from 1674-75. He first invested in the Company of Royal Adventurers in January 1663; by August, his holding had grown to two shares, worth £800. In January 1665, he bought a further £1,200 from the Countess of Chesterfield, and was elected to the company’s board where he served from 1667-70.

He continued attending board meetings, without formally serving, from 1671 until the company’s dissolution. This positioned him to invest heavily in the RAC, the Adventurers’ successor, subscribing with £5,000 (the equivalent of £1.18m today) and serving as an assistant from 1672-74. During his involvement with both companies, they undertook 81 crossings. Vyner left a portion of the remainder of his estate to Barts after his death in 1688.

Like St Thomas’ hospital in Lambeth, south London, Barts provided free medical care to the city’s sick and poor people, sustained by charitable donations from City merchants and rental income from land and property across the capital.

Last year, the stairwell leading to the Great Hall was restored and rehung with William Hogarth’s The Good Samaritan and The Pool of Bethesda. The hall’s baroque ceiling carries its own coded message, its botanical motifs – oak leaves for strength, laurel wreaths for triumph and palm branches for peace – all tied to themes of healthcare.

Barts has acknowledged its links to slavery: Barts health NHS trust archives produced an official research guide in 2024 setting out the known history and how to investigate it further, though the trust has not commissioned a stand-alone enslavement report.

A spokesperson for the trust said it was “well aware that some notable individuals historically associated with our hospitals profited from the transatlantic slave trade”, and they were identified in the Great Hall because of their donations.

“As further information comes to light we are discussing with Barts Charity and Barts Heritage, which manages the listed building, how we could most appropriately acknowledge the full story behind these historic links.”

A spokesperson for Barts Charity, which supports the trust, said that, previously, “detailed research has not established whether, or to what extent, particular gifts can be traced into the assets managed by the charity today. We are reviewing the new findings with Barts Health and Barts Heritage and considering any appropriate next steps.”

In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a ten-year restorative justice initiative.

rss_3_1789506146.title: Africa’s richest man aiming to make $23bn from continent’s biggest-ever IPO
rss_3_1789506146.text:
The fortune of Africa’s richest person could swell by two thirds to nearly $60bn (£44bn) after his refinery in Nigeria listed publicly in the continent’s biggest-ever initial public offering.

If Monday’s flotation of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals on the Nigerian exchange goes to plan, then Aliko Dangote will add a further $23bn (£17bn) to his $35bn net worth.

Dangote, who has framed the offering as “an IPO for the people”, hopes it will draw in a broad mix of institutional and retail investors with a minimum subscription of just 10 shares at a cost of 5,250 naira (£2.94). The share purchases have a month to complete, with the process finishing on 13 October.

The IPO has been marketed to young Nigerians in particular, through banking platforms and fintech ventures, as a way of building wealth and growing the economy. If completely subscribed, the refinery’s value is expected to rise to about 65.22tn naira (£36.5bn).

That would be a big win for Dangote, who has financed several successful presidential campaigns in Nigeria, where policymakers have granted him a near monopoly in his chosen sectors.

Responding last year to criticism of his political influence, he said: “We have chosen to build here, to employ here, to produce here. Let us not use the cry of monopoly to stall growth. No one is prevented from investing.”

Dangote, 69, made his fortune in cement and sugar. He started his company in the late 1970s with a loan from his maternal grandfather, who was a member of one of west Africa’s all-time richest families, the Dantatas.

His recent move into the petroleum sector led to Nigeria becoming a net exporter of refined fuel for the first time. Prior to the opening of the $20bn Dangote refinery on the outskirts of Lagos in January 2024, the country had relied on exporting crude and importing refined petroleum for domestic use, while expending billions to subsidise fuel costs and inject life into its colonial-era refineries.

The Dangote refinery now has a capacity of 700,000 barrels a day and is expected to double that by the end of the decade. This year, it has benefited from disruptions in supply across the globe as a result of the war in Iran. The Brent crude benchmark touched $108 a barrel on Monday, after attacks on Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline.

Dangote has said he will use profits from his Lagos oil refinery to spur continental growth and curb Africa’s reliance on foreign goods. His ambitious plan is to build a $100bn industrial empire centred on heavy manufacturing and regional infrastructure. Key to this is a planned $17bn energy complex in the Kenyan island town of Lamu with an oil-refining capacity of 700,000 barrels a day, to boost the region’s energy security.

“We, as Nigerians and Africans, must be bold and lead the change to develop our economies,” Dangote said at an IPO signing ceremony in Lagos on 7 September. “Only then will the others take us very seriously, only then we’ll be in a position to negotiate and walk away with terms we deserve, not those terms that are given to us.”

After the ceremony, Dangote’s fellow Nigerian billionaire, the banker Tony Elumelu, called the IPO “a landmark moment for Nigeria and a huge milestone for Africa”.

rss_4_1789506147.title: Burial of King Oyo takes place in Uganda as news anchor prepares for throne
rss_4_1789506147.text:
Uganda’s King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, long the world’s youngest monarch, has been buried among the tombs of his royal forebears as ⁠his Tooro kingdom looked to put ⁠a bitter succession battle behind ​it.

Oyo’s appointed successor, the news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma, cast nine coffee berries into the grave at the Karambi Royal Tombs, marking the formal handover of power in the western Ugandan kingdom.

Oyo made global headlines in 1995 when he took the throne at the age of three. Images of the toddler king wearing a crown and royal robes sparked curiosity and adoration around the world.

View image in fullscreen King Oyo of the Toro kingdom was for a long time the world’s youngest monarch. Photograph: Sipa/Shutterstock

He died last month at 34 ⁠in the United States, where he was receiving treatment for cancer.

Uganda is led by an elected head of state but retains several kingdoms that pre-date the ​British colonial era and are regarded as bulwarks of traditional identity ‌and heritage.

At a church service before ‌the burial, Oyo, who became a UN goodwill ambassador championing the fight against HIV and Aids, was eulogised as a reserved but jovial young man.

“Although ‌he became king and carried responsibilities far beyond what most people ever experience, he never completely lost the young boy who loved to have fun,” said his sister, Ruth Komuntale.

Royal guards clad in orange shawls then led the hearse carrying Oyo’s casket through the streets of the kingdom’s capital, Fort Portal, to the royal tombs, as thousands of mourners joined the procession on foot.

The burial, which was held 31 years to the day after Oyo’s coronation, followed days of bickering within the notoriously fractious royal family.

A committee consisting of members ‌of the royal clan announced on Wednesday it had chosen Oyo’s cousin, Kijanangoma, a news anchor and editor at state broadcaster UBC, as king.

But the late king’s immediate family said his hitherto unknown son should succeed him, as called ​for in his will. Oyo never married and was not known to have any children until the kingdom’s prime minister said in the statement announcing his death that he had a son.

View image in fullscreen UBC news anchor Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma. Photograph: UBC Uganda

Supporters of Kijanangoma’s succession say Oyo’s family has not been able to produce basic information about the purported son.

A source with knowledge of crisis talks over the matter said Ugandan authorities had successfully pushed through Kijanangoma’s succession on Friday. A government spokesperson could not be reached for comment.

The archbishop of the ⁠Church of Uganda, Stephen Kaziimba Mugalu, called for unity.

“Words spoken in grief can cause pain, division and conflict,” he ​told mourners. “It can even destroy the legacy ​of the king we are mourning.”

Oyo himself took the throne after a protracted succession battle that finished in court.

In ​addition to his ceremonial responsibilities and campaigning ‌against HIV and Aids, ​Oyo cultivated close ties with former ​Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi, whom he named a special adviser to the monarch. Gaddafi donated money towards refurbishment of the royal palace.

The 56-year-old Kijanangoma, who maintained a low profile as the succession battle played out, has been described by fellow Ugandan journalists as quiet and humble.

Besides the throne, the new king will inherit a considerable royal estate including swathes of land and sizeable cash payouts from the central government.

rss_5_1789506147.title: Ferocious fight among Brazil’s supreme court erupts on eve of presidential election
rss_5_1789506147.text:
Brazil’s supreme court has been thrust into what experts consider the greatest crisis since the return of democracy in the 1980s, as two rival judges lock horns on the eve of the presidential election with unpredictable consequences for Latin America’s largest democracy.

The politically charged dispute exploded into public view on Tuesday as judges traded insults and accusations during a heated supreme court hearing that was livestreamed into millions of Brazilian homes.

During one of the most ferocious exchanges, one of the judges at the eye of the storm, Alexandre de Moraes, berated his rival, André Mendonça: “You’re at the service of a political group that tried to launch a coup in this country!”

“It’s a lie!” Mendonça cried back.

Minutes later, a third judge, Gilmar Mendes, angrily accused Mendonça of weaponizing the court’s work to cause political chaos and influence October’s presidential election.

“Don’t point your finger at me, Minister Gilmar! Don’t point your finger! You’re not talking to any old person! Show some respect to this court!” Mendonça warned Mendes, who shot back: “Respect is earned, not given.”

The courtroom drama – in many ways a proxy for the electoral battle between the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro – pits Moraes, a pugnacious shaven-headed martial arts practitioner, against Mendonça, a Presbyterian pastor who is the only openly evangelical member of the 11-seat court.

Moraes was appointed almost a decade ago by rightwing president Michel Temer. But the 57-year-old judge is widely associated with Lula thanks to his successful prosecution of Flávio Bolsonaro’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for plotting a botched coup after losing the 2022 election to the leftwing veteran.

Mendonça, meanwhile, was named during Jair Bolsonaro’s 2018-23 presidency and leftwingers widely view him as a stooge for the disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his failed power grab.

With less than three weeks to go until the election, the two judges have gone to war, as Brazil’s biggest-ever banking scandal has snowballed into a judicial and political crisis of similarly shocking proportions.

The Banco Master scandal began last November when the playboy owner of that collapsed bank, Daniel Vorcaro, was arrested by federal police as he prepared to board a private jet from São Paulo to Malta.

Investigations uncovered apparent links between the jailed banker and an astonishing panoply of figures from Brazil’s political and judicial elite, foremost among them Flávio Bolsonaro and Moraes. Other members of the supreme court and their relatives have also been linked to Vorcaro.

Mendonça has been accused of deliberately fast-tracking the investigation into Moraes, while stalling the inquiry into Vorcaro’s ties to the Bolsonaros and the banker’s bankrolling of a film about Jair Bolsonaro.

Earlier this month, Mendonça unsealed an explosive police dossier relating to the Banco Master investigation that contained compromising WhatsApp exchanges apparently between Vorcaro and Moraes as well as a copy of a $25m contract between Banco Master and the law firm of Moraes’s wife. In one text message, sent two days before his arrest, Vorcaro asked Moraes: “Do you think … I need to get out [of the country]?”

Moraes hit back on the eve of Tuesday’s hearing, claiming he was being smeared with politically-motivated “criminal lies” as part of a revenge attack by the rightwing forces behind the coup attempt that culminated in the January 2023 riots in Brasília. Moraes also alleged that the attacks on him involved “external actors” and were part of a possible foreign attempt to interfere in Brazil’s election.

The Moraes/Mendonça tussle reached a crescendo on Tuesday as supreme court judges convened in Brasília to decide whether an investigation should be opened into Moraes’s conduct. Moraes has demanded an investigation into Mendonça.

The judicial scandal has exploded just as Brazil’s election campaign is coming to a head, with polls suggesting a dead heat between Lula and Bolsonaro, who are likely to face off in a second-round run-off on 25 October.

“The timing is awful. We are just a few weeks away from elections that already look to be challenging for a democracy that has been struggling to deal with extremist and anti-democratic groups that continue to be an important political force in the country. So I think we have a perfect storm here,” said Eloísa Machado, a constitutional law professor who follows the supreme court.

Machado said Lula had “absolutely nothing to do” with the scandal engulfing Moraes and the supreme court, noting how the leftwing president had not appointed the judge.

Even so, the crisis looks likely to hurt Lula’s chances of winning a historic fourth term, given the widespread public association between him and Moraes because of the judge’s involvement in Jair Bolsonaro’s jailing.

In a social media video posted as Tuesday’s hearing played out, Flávio Bolsonaro blamed the judicial scandal on Lula’s administration but made no mention of his own alleged ties to Vorcaro.

“This [is happening] because the current government ... is part of this decaying system and we are now seeing this rotten system reveal itself before the eyes of the entire nation,” Bolsonaro said, claiming Lula had “shared power” with Moraes.

Thomas Traumann, a political analyst, predicted the scandal would accelerate the election campaign’s descent into a carnival of mudslinging, as both sides battled to convince voters of their rival’s sins.

“This campaign is going to get dirtier much faster than we had expected,” he said.

rss_6_1789506147.title: Carney says Canada will pursue ‘unique security and economic alliance’ with EU amid US trade spat
rss_6_1789506147.text:
Mark Carney said Canada will pursue a “unique security and economic alliance” with Europe as he positions his country as a base to build in the “new global economic order”.

Speaking to investors, company executives and government ministers at the inaugural Canada Investment Summit on Tuesday, the prime minister pitched Canada as a “safe harbour” and lucrative home for foreign capital as his government looks to reduce its reliance on trade with the United States.

Over the last 18 months, the relationship with the US has fractured, leaving Canada searching for ways to avert economic devastation.

“The world is becoming more divided and dangerous. Sovereignty and openness are now in tension. Economic integration is being weaponised. Tariffs are used as leverage,” Carney said – a nod to the Donald Trump’s penchant for trade levies.

“Canada recognised the rupture earlier than most. Our response reflects the two lessons we have taken from it: First, we must take care of ourselves, and second, we must take care of each other. Taking care of ourselves means building our strength at home and diversifying our partnerships abroad.”

While Carney has referred to the trade spat as a “war”, there was a duelling sense of optimism at the summit among senior Canadian officials that the country’s more global perspective could usher in hundreds of billions in fresh investment into the country.

That shift has been exemplified in recent weeks by Carney’s effort to strengthen Canada’s economic and political ties to the EU. Noting in his remarks at the summit that Canada is the only non-European member of Europe’s defence procurement initiative, the prime minister said his government will pursue a “unique” relationship with the bloc. He mused about the range of possibilities, including the prospect of visa-free travel and work between the two that has been raised in recent days, but said Canada and the EU were in early stage of talks.

Carney will be the guest of honour at the European parliament’s plenary meeting in Strasbourg this week. He will attend European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s annual state of the union speech on Wednesday, where she is expected to sketch out new areas for EU-Canada cooperation. On Thursday, Carney will address MEPs in von der Leyen’s presence. The commission president hastily changed her plans to stay in Strasbourg, after being criticised over her initial “unacceptable” decision to skip Carney’s speech and return to Brussels.

European officials are seeking to bring Canada as close as possible to the EU short of membership. But it will not be called associate membership, as the EU seeks to maintain a clear distinction between members and nonmembers. The long experience of Brexit negotiations cemented the EU’s preference not to split the four freedoms of its single market – free movement of people, services, goods and capital – so any deepening of the Canada relationship will be built around this red line. More immediately, the EU hopes to improve ties on raw materials and energy.

Javier Moreno Sánchez, a Spanish socialist MEP, who leads the European parliament’s Canada delegation, said he wanted to hear “concrete steps” from von der Leyen on how to improve the EU-Canada relationship, calling for greater mobility for professionals, more student exchanges, joint work on defence and artificial intelligence.

“Canadians are the most European people outside Europe and that is the key point for the development of our relationship,” he said. “Due to the difficult geopolitical geoeconomic situation in the world and the difficult relationship we have, both Canada and the European Union, with our traditional partner, the United States, I think it is the moment to have a closer relationship with Canada.”

The EU and Canada already have a wide-ranging relationship, including a free-trade agreement and separate deals on digital cooperation, raw materials, research and a shared green alliance. Earlier this year, Canada became the first non-European country to join the EU’s €150bn defence loans scheme, meaning greater opportunities for Canadian defence firms to supply Europe.

But irritants persist. Ten EU member states, including France, Italy and Poland, have not ratified the landmark EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) nearly a decade after it was signed, meaning parts of the deal are yet to enter into force.

French lawmaker Valérie Hayer, Emmanuel Macron’s ally in the European parliament, acknowledged the problem. “In the French parliament this agreement has yet to be ratified, notwithstanding the [trade] figures which are extremely good. That is why I call on political leaders [in France] to do their bit to act responsibly as elsewhere to make sure that we [the EU] can count for more in world affairs.”

Hayer’s centrist Renew group, only the fifth-largest in the European parliament, is calling on EU member states and the commission to speed up Ceta ratification and launch an awareness-raising drive so European and Canadian companies have better knowledge of the trade opportunities. But ahead of a year of big elections – in France, Italy and Poland – progress on ratifying the 10-year-old agreement looks uncertain.

EU-Canada’s trade in goods and services hit €130bn in 2025, an 80% increase since 2016 when Ceta was signed. But this pales in comparison to trade with the US, which is worth nearly US$880bn.

Despite a deliberate push to increase global trade, Carney acknowledged the geographic realities of Canada’s proximity to its southern neighbour, and the reality, which most economists concede, that the US will remain Canada’s largest trading partner.

“We will always be neighbours, and Canada will continue to be the US’s most important partner in many key areas,” he said. These arrangements work when we engage as true partners that respect each other’s traditions and sovereignty.”

In recent weeks, Trump has both threatened Canada’s economy and mused about a North America under the umbrella of an expanded US.

Event host Erik Schatzker told attendees that Canada was neither a “bystander nor a victim” in the dramatic geopolitical shifts that have defined the Trump era. “Canada is a protagonist. Canada has agency. Canada is defining its own future.”

Carney said foreign investment has dramatically increased and the federal government was on track to balance the operating budget one year ahead of schedule, an announcement that received applause from the crowd. He announced a corporate tax “mega-deduction” that would help compete with similar incentives in the US allowing companies to immediately deduct 100% of the cost of new investment across more assets than previously permitted.

Carney also confirmed Canada would open four of its major airports to foreign investment in order to “unlock their true value”. The prime minister also said his government would “apply [the] lessons” of instances in which allowing partial private investment had failed.

But that theme – soliciting hundreds of billions in foreign investment while also reshoring domestic capability – has frustrated some.

Ahead of the summit, thousands gathered in downtown Toronto for the Many vs the Money counter protest. Organisers said public money should not be used to reduce the risks of private investment while communities are left to shoulder the social and environmental costs of these projects.

“Mark Carney’s here selling Canada to the international community,” said Stephen Hill, a lone protester standing outside the hotel as key figures arrived to the prime minister’s speech. “I’m Canadian. We’re an Aboriginal-led investment coalition. We want in. But you can’t get a returned email. You can’t get a returned phone call. You can’t get through to his ministers. So I’m here from British Columbia to try and get his attention and to tell him to think of Canadians first.”

Ahead of Tuesday’s summit, the prime minister’s office announced nearly C$500bn in new domestic investment.

“Canada has what the world wants,” Carney said during media availability late Tuesday morning. “The difference, this week, is that we didn’t cross an ocean to make our case. The world came to us … but what matters most is what we do for ourselves.”

rss_7_1789506147.title: Panama canal traffic to be cut again as drought from El Niño worsens
rss_7_1789506147.text:
The Panama canal plans to again cut maritime traffic due to worsening drought caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon, further choking up one of the world’s most important shipping lanes.

The canal handles 5% of global maritime trade and about 40% of US container traffic; it is favoured by shippers because it usually reduces cost and transit times, especially for companies trading between China, Asia and the US.

From October, an average of 29.5 vessels will be allowed to transit daily – down 18% from 36 in August, according to a draft plan submitted to Panama’s parliament. In September, officials cut daily transits from 36 to 32 because of the drought.

The US and Israel’s war on Iran, and its disruption to the strait of Hormuz, has complicated logistics and added costs for shipping companies using the canal.

In August, with vessels waiting 10 days to enter the canal – the longest since May – a container ship reportedly paid about $4m (£3m) to jump the queue. Maritime companies usually pay a flat fee to reserve a slot to transit the canal, but a daily auction allows shipowners to place bids to skip the queue. Bid prices generally rise during high demand.

Shipping restrictions on the canal could yet worsen, with El Niño expected to peak later this year. The natural weather pattern that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns is forecast to be the strongest in four decades.

The 82km-long canal, connecting the Caribbean Sea to the Pacific Ocean, relies on fresh water from rivers pouring into Lake Gatun to operate its system of locks. In September, officials said the watershed had received lower than forecast rainfall.

The canal’s locks act like elevators, each filling with water to lift ships 26 metres (85 feet) from sea level to Lake Gatun and then back down to sea level on the other side.

If lake levels are no longer safe for the largest ships to pass, the Panama Canal Authority imposes restrictions for safety and to preserve water.

In 2023 the water level in the lakes feeding the canal was so low authorities cut daily transits from 38 to 22. Those restrictions led to a bottleneck of ships and sent companies scrambling to find alternative routes.

El Niño has severely affected Central America and northern parts of South America, where nine countries have experienced their hottest June-August period on record this year.

Fifty-two countries across all continents broke their seasonal temperature records for that period, according to an Agence France-Presse analysis of meteorological data from the European Copernicus programme.

The extreme heat has taken many forms, from unprecedented heatwaves in Europe to devastating drought in Sudan and toxic smoke in Indonesia.

More than a third of people experiencing the hottest northern summer months on record were in Africa, particularly in the Sahel and areas south of it.

Eighteen African countries broke their seasonal records for the June-August period, from Mauritania and Sierra Leone in the west to Eritrea and Ethiopia in the east.

rss_8_1789506147.title: ‘A coin flip’: on the campaign trail as Brazil’s far right edges back to power
rss_8_1789506147.text:
A giant banner of Brazil’s incarcerated former president Jair Bolsonaro fluttered in the morning breeze as his eldest son, Flávio, touched down at an airfield on the fringe of a city that will soon help decide the future of one of the biggest democracies on earth.

“Brazil is rudderless. Brazil has no president and Brazil needs a president – and that president is Flávio Bolsonaro,” the far-right senator declared as he waded into the flock of supporters who had gathered to welcome him to Juiz de Fora, one of the largest cities in the battleground state of Minas Gerais.

With less than a month before nearly 159 million Brazilians choose their next leader on 4 October, the election appears on a knife-edge, with the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro, neck-and-neck in the polls.

View image in fullscreen Bolsonaro supporters float a giant balloon depicting the US president, Donald Trump, holding Brazil’s president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Photograph: Miguel Schincariol/AFP/Getty Images

Bolsonaro’s campaign appears to have seized the momentum in recent weeks amid a slew of corruption scandals involving Lula’s son and the supreme court. That has prompted despair among progressives who fear their country could fall back into the hands of a radical rightwing movement that tried to grab power after the then-president, Jair Bolsonaro, lost the 2022 election to Lula.

Last September, Jair Bolsonaro received a 27-year jail sentence for spearheading that botched coup – a verdict supporters insist was unjust. But the ex-president and his accomplices are likely to be freed if his son wins power – a prospect that delights the hardcore Bolsonaristas who turned out to greet Flávio Bolsonaro wearing yellow football shirts and headbands reading: “Lula out!”

“Today is a moment of joy,” said Ulisses Lima, 50, a cybersecurity specialist with a Jesus Christ pendant around his neck. “Flávio represents change. He represents Brazil’s rescue from this socialist abyss we’ve spent so long warning about,” Lima added as supporters waited for the former president’s heir to arrive.

View image in fullscreen Brazil’s president Lula at a reelection campaign rally in Curitiba on Saturday. Photograph: Rodolfo Bührer/Reuters

Nearby, another devotee, José Caldeira, fell to his knees and begged for divine intervention to get Bolsonaro out of house arrest. “God, free this nation! Amnesty and freedom for Bolsonaro!” Caldeira bellowed, raising his hands towards the sky.

A third man, Davi Frederico, held a banner celebrating Donald Trump, who has been accused of trying to swing the election in Bolsonaro’s favour through economic and diplomatic pressure. “Make Liberals Cry Again,” it said.

Juiz de Fora, an industrial and university city traditionally associated with the left, is also a key location for Brazil’s hard right. The city’s army headquarters was the launchpad for the 1964 coup that plunged Brazil into two decades of military rule. And it was in Juiz de Fora, on the eve of the 2018 election, that Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in the gut while campaigning – an attack widely believed to have helped the former paratrooper seal his victory.

View image in fullscreen Davi Frederico at the airport in Juiz de Fora. Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

Bolsonaro’s shock win ushered in what, from a progressive perspective, were four abysmal years. Destruction of the Amazon rainforest and gun ownership skyrocketed, hundreds of thousands died during a Covid outbreak Bolsonaro was accused of mishandling, and the president’s authoritarian rhetoric and attacks on Brazil’s electronic voting system culminated in the 8 January 2023 riots in Brasília. The supreme court later called those disturbances part of a plot to “annihilate” the country’s democracy.

But the Bolsonaros still enjoy abundant support, and that devotion was visible as Flávio Bolsonaro’s motorcade crept towards the high street where his father was ambushed eight years ago.

View image in fullscreen Street hawkers at Flavio Bolsonaro’s campaign event pay tribute to the US connection. Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

“Let’s get the left out! Let’s get these motherfuckers out!” one elderly woman shrieked as the senator passed by on top of a sound truck stamped with the word: “Jesus”. Other fans, many senior citizens, waved Brazil flags from windows or stood on the sidewalk flashing victory signs with their hands.

“Barring some kind of leftwing trickery, Flávio Bolsonaro can already be considered president. All you have to do is take a look at the streets and social media,” claimed Nikolas Ferreira, an influential far-right congressman from Minas Gerais who has more than 9 million TikTok followers.

Alongside the enthusiasm, there were glimpses of the revulsion many Brazilians feel for the former president. One leftwinger took to his balcony with a loudhailer to taunt the Bolsonaristas as they paraded through town. “Trump! Trump! Get my daddy out of jail!” the dissenter jeered in reference to the US president’s attempts to help Bolsonaro escape punishment.

View image in fullscreen Supporters gather to greet Flávio Bolsonaro at Juiz de Fora, Minas Gerais. Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing here. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate in Minas by more than 1.7m votes. Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000. After landing in Minas last week, Flávio Bolsonaro said he was confident of clawing back the swing state, with one recent poll putting him ahead there.

“[Lula] is a president who you look at and see the past,” the 45-year-old senator said of his 80-year-old adversary. “With Flávio you can be sure that when people look at him, they see a modern government and a government of the future.”

Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has written a book about his polarised country, said the election was too close to call. “It’s a coin flip,” said Traumann, who believed an unexpected scandal or last-minute “black swan” event could swing the election either way. On Friday, it emerged that Flávio Bolsonaro had been placed under police investigation over suspicions of corruption involving the funding of a big-budget biopic telling the story of the assassination attempt against his father in Juiz de Fora.

View image in fullscreen Flávio Bolsonaro addresses supporters at the spot where Jair Bolsonaro was stabbed in Juiz de Fora during the 2018 presidential campaign. Photograph: Pablo Porciúncula/AFP/Getty Images

For progressive voters, the vision for a Flávio Bolsonaro administration laid out during his visit to Minas is the stuff of nightmares. “I think Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidency is going to be Jair Bolsonaro 2.0,” said Bruno Engler, a Bolsonarista lawmaker from Minas’ capital, Belo Horizonte.

Engler believed a top priority would be zero-tolerance policing, with the younger Bolsonaro pledging an iron-fisted crackdown on criminals his father has compared to cockroaches. “Thugs who don’t surrender will be arrested or neutralised,” Engler vowed, predicting gun laws would be loosened.

Speaking on the street corner where his father was knifed, Flávio Bolsonaro vowed to pack Brazil’s 11-member supreme court with five conservative judges “who are against abortion [and] against drugs”. “We’re going to give the streets back to the Brazilian people … We’re going to lower the age of criminal responsibility. We are going to introduce chemical castration for rapists,” shouted the candidate, who wore a bullet-proof vest.

Those pledges prompted whoops of excitement from the crush of supporters below Bolsonaro’s truck. Dozens ofmobile phones captured the candidate’s every word. But amid the rightwing rejoicing there was fear and trepidation, too.

View image in fullscreen Lennon César: ‘Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.’ Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

Lennon César, a law student and leftwing activist who had come to confront Bolsonaro’s fans, voiced incredulity that less than four years after Jair Bolsonaro’s failed power grab, tens of millions of Brazilians seemed poised to vote for his son.

“We were the victims of an attempted coup – and his father was the perpetrator,” recalled César, 28. “It’s terrifying. And the thing that worries me most is that the general public doesn’t really seem to get what’s happening. Brazilians have short memories when it comes to the past.”

As a black, gay man, César felt particular dread at the prospect of a second Bolsonaro presidency, given the patriarch’s hostility to minorities.

César vowed to vote for Lula, Brazil’s first working-class president, calling him the only leader who paid attention to the poor. “If today I’m studying for a law degree it’s because one of Lula’s government programmes allowed me to achieve that,” he said, warning: “These people … might destroy it all.”

A few blocks away, a graffiti artist had spray painted their own message of disapproval on to the facade of Bolsonaro’s Juiz de Fora HQ. “Facists [sic],” it read.

rss_9_1789506148.title: Canada offers air defense support for Ukraine as Zelenskyy visits
rss_9_1789506148.text:
Canada offered support on Thursday to boost Ukraine’s air defenses and help replenish its drone stocks, as the countries pledged to deepen their alliance during a visit by Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Mark Carney hosted the president of Ukraine in Calgary in the western province of Alberta, where the Canadian prime minister grew up among a large community of people with Ukrainian heritage.

“Canada will always be with you,” Carney assured Zelenskyy.

The leaders signed an agreement to work toward a “hundred-year partnership”.

That deal, to be negotiated over the coming months, aims to codify cooperation in a range of areas, including defense, critical minerals and energy.

“Our two nations have been connected since 1893,” Carney said, referring to a wave of Ukrainians who migrated to the new Canadian nation.

In Alberta, there are an estimated 350,000 Canadians of Ukrainian descent.

“Ukrainians helped build Canada and Canadians will help rebuild Ukraine,” Carney said.

The support announced on Thursday includes C$350m (US$253m) provided through the United States’ Joint Ukraine Multinational Program – Services, Training and Articles Rapid Timeline (Jumpstart) program.

Zelenskyy has emphasized the need for increased air defense as Russia ramps up ballistic missile attacks.

Carney said Canada was also offering C$450m in loan guarantees to enhance the Ukrainian energy supply.

The funds will help repair damaged infrastructure, increase storage capacity and improve power supply to hospitals.

Carney said the goal of the energy support was “to help Ukrainians get through the winter”, a difficult period when the country endures rolling blackouts amid often frigid temperatures.

Canada is moving aggressively to increase its own drone stocks, Carney said, announcing a deal that will see 30% of new Canadian production head to Ukraine.

Zelenskyy told reporters that “these drones will go to Ukraine immediately to [the] battlefield, immediately to our people, our soldiers … to save our children, our families first of all.”

Asked about potential negotiations to ease the fighting, Zelenskyy said he did not anticipate any substantive talks during Russia’s ongoing election period.

But he said he planned to meet Donald Trump in New York City in late September, probably on the sidelines of the UN general assembly, with Washington bidding to revive long-stalled talks to end the war.

“But at the end of September, we will have an opportunity to meet, I think, with the American team in New York,” Zelenskyy said.

“And I think that … I can be more open after the New York meeting with President Trump.”

After the Calgary meeting, Zelenskyy was headed to Banff, a stunning Canadian national park, where he will address a cabinet retreat for Carney’s liberal government.

He then heads to Canada’s largest city, Toronto, and North Bay in northern Ontario.
